bib.title: The Red Queen Gödel Machine: Co-Evolving Agents and Their Evaluators

legacy_report:
SOURCE: The Red Queen Godel Machine: Co-Evolving Agents and Their Evaluators. Iacob, Jovanovic, et al. Preprint, 2026. File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/04-loop-engineering/sources/iacob-2026-red-queen-godel-machine.pdf

COVERAGE: Pages 18-40 read in full (pypdf, clean text, no garbling). References (pp. 10-16) skimmed for the 15 entries listed in BUILDS ON. Pages 1-9 (main text) and 17 (TOC) NOT re-read, because the previous pass covered them; I looked only at their first lines. Pages read: 23 of 40 in full, plus a partial skim of 10-16 (so 24-30/40 by a generous count; say 23/40 full, 7/40 skimmed, 10/40 not read).

CLAIMS (new or qualifying; ranked)
- Theory holds only per epoch and rests on stationarity. Assumption 1 (C2) needs binary outcomes with time-invariant success probability; Asm. 2 needs the evaluator, workspace, sampling protocol and scoring rule fixed within an epoch. "The task-agent objective changes at every transition, so this statement is per epoch." (p.37). The theory proves no guarantee across epochs for the agent objective.
  quote: "Item C2 is the one RQGM must work to keep. HGM relies on a fixed evaluator for it" (p.35)
- Prop 1: pooled Beta mean converges a.s. to epoch-local utility, if cell counts converge to weights and each cell's rate converges (e.g. independent Bernoulli). Error bound 1/(n+2). Prop 2: selective erasure preserves criterion consistency. Prop 3 and 5: each epoch is a fixed binary-outcome search, so HGM Theorem 1 applies per epoch. Theorem 1 itself is HGM's (Wang et al.): "access to a CMP oracle is sufficient to implement the Godel Machine within the given search budget" (p.34), under Asm. 1.
- Prop 4: the best-belief (epsilon-quantile of Beta) lower bound holds with prob 1-eps per selection, and all L bounds hold with prob >= 1-L*eps (union bound), assuming each selected agent's violation probability is <= eps under the joint data and selection process. eps=0.05, 5-outcome anchor minimum (Tab. 4). Note the selection-bias caveat is assumed away, not proved.
- Prop 6: exponential checkpoints (rho=2) reprocess at most rho*B/(rho-1) = 2B records; uniform dense checkpointing is Theta(B^2/h). Assumes each evaluation writes at most one slot-dependent record.
- Props 7-8: with exact validation, replacement strictly raises anchor accuracy Q and stops after at most N replacements (N equally weighted items). With noisy best-belief, Q(new) >= max Q - 2*eta_j. Beta quantile within 1/sqrt(4(n+3)min(eps,1-eps)) of the mean (Eq. 3).
  Adversarial objective: Q_P(e)=p+/2 + p-/4 + r_P/4. Because the pool changes between checkpoints, the guarantee weakens to Q_{j+1}(e_{j+1}) >= Q_j(e_j) - 2*eta_j - delta_j (Eq. 4), where delta_j is the pool drift. So with a pool there is NO monotone improvement guarantee. "The anchor terms p+ and p- never change, so the adversarial term only reweights it."
- Guarantees concern the validation anchor, not the true objective: "The guarantee concerns the validation objective and survives any shortlist containing the incumbent." (p.38)
- Mechanism ablations. Paper domain (Tab. 11, Nemotron 3 Super, 12,288 evals): the fixed reviewer saturates, with writer validation 100.0 +-1.7 but reviewer anchor accuracy only 78.2 +-4.4. Full mechanism: reviewer anchor 95.0 +-10.3. Replacement only: 91.2 +-7.4. No erasure: 92.9 +-10.8. Intervals overlap, so the pool's and erasure's separate contributions on the reviewer are not statistically separated. Text: "Without the fixed reviewer... the writer ends with all 75 validation papers accepted". Without erasure "replacements stop as outdated evidence accumulates".
  quote: "Fixed reviewer off off - 100.0+-1.7 78.2+-4.4" (p.27)
- Proof ablations (Nemotron 3 Ultra, Tab. 12, 0-7 score, 95% problem-cluster bootstrap): full 3.60 [2.55,4.67]; pool off 3.14 [2.13,4.20]; transitions off 2.64 [1.74,3.55]; coupled HGM 3.05 [2.11,4.04]. Intervals overlap heavily. Grader (Tab. 13, 548 items, 20 problems): exact agreement full 67.3% [57.6,76.9], coupled HGM 65.7% [55.9,75.1], pool off 58.8, transitions off 56.0; MAE/7 0.122 vs 0.141 (HGM). Full vs coupled HGM is within noise. Proof ablation uses a 1,024-evaluation budget, not 12,288 (p.21).
- Proof held-out per grader (Tab. 10): the RQGM specialist's 4.95 mean (70% P@6, 60% P@7) is under the RQGM grader, which co-evolved with it. Excluding that grader, the two independent graders give 4.03 vs 4.08 for static IMO25 and 3.60 for HGM-H. So the specialist does not beat the static IMO25 prover under independent graders. Quote: "Excluding the RQGM grader, which co-evolved with the specialist, the two independent graders give it 4.03, against 4.08 for IMO25 and 3.60 for HGM-H." (p.26). Under ProofAutoGrader: IMO25 4.05, HGM-H 3.55, RQGM specialist 3.85, generalist 3.55. P@7: specialist trails IMO25 (40 vs 55). N=60 outcomes (20 problems x 3 graders).
- Reviewer held-out (Tab. 8, 100 APReS papers): HGM-H specialist 88% acc / 45% accept; RQGM specialist 84 / 40; RQGM generalist 84 / 42; RQGM adversarial 80 / 32; DGM-H published 73 / 25; Sakana prompt 63 / 13. So HGM-H's reviewer beats RQGM's on accuracy (88 vs 84). Polyglot coder: RQGM 71.7% vs HGM-H 69.9% (166 tasks, a 1.8-point gap, no interval given).
- DeepSWE (Tab. 9, 28 held-out tasks): RQGM coder 82.1/85.7/85.7 (low/medium/high) vs HGM-H 75.0/78.6/82.1 vs GPT-6 Astra base 68.8/76.8/83.0. At high effort the base model (83.0) beats the RQGM coder (85.7) by only 2.7 points, and HGM-H (82.1) is below the base. The reference is the mean of 4 attempts. Base xhigh and max are 80.4, so effort is not monotone. n=28 means one task is 3.6 points. Search tokens to winner: 587M (RQGM) vs 429M (HGM-H) (Tab. 6).
- Cost (Tab. 14, M blended tokens): RQGM full run 2,876.8 (validation 1,948.2, train 821.4, expansion 107.3); HGM-H full 2,532.7. Validation is 65-70% of tokens (GPT-5.5 runs, 65-69%); expansion 18-23%; train 12-14%. RQGM costs about 14% more tokens than HGM-H in total for DeepSWE.
- Anchor transfer to search (Tab. 15, DeepSWE): reviewers seated before the last accepted nearly every patch (e.g. 100.0% of failing patches accepted at anchor 0.22; 92.9% at 0.22). Only the final reviewer (anchor 0.48) separates: accepts 35.0% passing vs 20.8% failing (as printed; the text says 47% passing vs 19% failing on 337 jointly-judged patches, balanced accuracy 0.52 to 0.64, 95% bootstrap interval of the drop [0.12,0.80]). Seated anchors: 0.03, 0.12, 0.19, 0.22 ... 0.48. Replaced 11 times across 8 distinct reviewers. Takeaway: anchor score 0.22 reviewers gave "almost no signal"; the final reviewer is still weak (balanced accuracy 0.64).
- Cost-reduction: Nemotron 3 Ultra for search-time task-agent calls gives about 13x lower price-equivalent cost "while nearly matching" GPT-5.5-only accuracy (Fig. 12, accuracy axis 78-84%). Derivation: cost = 0.20B + 0.80(0.10B) = 0.28B (about 3.6x on that formula; the 13x figure comes from the token-count difference, selected reviewer B=6.68M costs 1.87M equivalent). Prices $5/$30 vs $0.5/$2.2 per M tokens.
- Reward design (Genesis, Go2 quadruped, PPO 4,096 envs, 101 iters): 5 searches per arm, 125 evals; 6 held-out jumping rewards per run; threshold 0.3494 m torso height. Curriculum arm 291 PPO trainings and 53.8M tokens vs static 325 and 48.3M. Cost $24-27 vs HyperAgents about $104 (3.85-4.33x reduction; this compares different models, Nemotron 3 Ultra vs Claude Sonnet 4.5). Held-out results are in Tab. 1 (main text, not re-read).
- Patch surfaces: shared task-agent code and infrastructure carry 59-90% of accepted patches in every GPT-5.5 run; 83% of RQGM DeepSWE code patches modify shared code or both roles (52 accepted code patches; archives of 82 vs 73 nodes). Largest single-step gain in any winning chain: grader alignment at node 22 (proof). Node 66 turned the inherited proof revision pass off by default and added "Preserve the draft if it is essentially sound".
- Evolved evaluator behaviour: a one-line instruction became a rubric; the search's most common move is rubric writing. Polyglot code reviewer replaced 3 times, each narrowing failure to "a concrete blocker" and "If evidence is balanced, prefer pass" (leniency). Adversarial reviewer: "conjunctive" selective-conference standard; displaced generalist: two-sided calibration. DeepSWE reviewer evolved from a single call to reading the repo, a checklist written before seeing the patch, and applying the patch to a scratch copy with Git.
- Setup constants (Tab. 4): 12,288 evaluations per run; eps=0.05; power-of-two checkpoints (rho=2); UCB-Air alpha=0.6; 3 train samples per node; 100-item test sets; Polyglot 10/49/166 train/val/test. DeepSWE: 28/57/28 tasks, alpha=2/3 then 1/2 after 600 evals, GPT-6 Astra (high) meta-agent, (low) task agents. Wang et al. used 8,000 evaluations for one task. Eight headline runs, one seed each (no repeats stated).
- Initial agents (C.9): every task agent is one LLM call from a shared template "You are an agent. Task input: ... {output_format}"; the only engineered prompts are the control baselines (Sakana reviewer, ProofAutoGrader). The meta-agent "is never shown any validation outcomes during the search" and reads only ancestors' train-split predictions, transcripts and diffs.

LIMITS (from G and elsewhere)
- Authors concede: stationarity within epoch can break with "provider-side model updates or nondeterministic tools"; generated papers/proofs scored by automated panels, not human experts; the anchor bounds what evolution can achieve ("A weak, noisy, or biased anchor lets evaluators drift across epochs"; a good anchor "confines them to its own decision boundary, so gains beyond the benchmark must come from objectives layered on top of it"); APReS and IMO-GradingBench grades are imperfect.
- Not shown: any guarantee across epochs or on the true objective; bounds on adversarial-pool drift delta_j; independence assumption for Prop 4 selection bias; multiple seeds; human-judged quality; DeepSWE n=28; ablation intervals overlap.
- Dated: models (GPT-5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Nemotron 3) and pricing are 2026 snapshots.

BUILDS ON: Schmidhuber 2003 (Godel machines); Zhang, Hu, Lu, Lange, Clune (Darwin Godel Machine, ICLR 2026) [1]; Wang et al. (Huxley-Godel Machine, ICLR 2026) [2], whose CMP, Thompson sampling and Theorem 1 are reused; Zhang et al. (HyperAgents, arXiv 2603.19461, 2026) [3]; Wang, Audibert, Munos 2008 (UCB-Air, infinitely many-armed bandits) [24]; APReS, Zhao et al. 2026 [25]; CRAVE dataset (Zhang, L., 2025) [27]; DeepSWE, Huang et al. 2026 [13]; Zheng et al. 2023 (LLM-as-a-judge) [15]; Skalse et al. 2022 (reward gaming) [17]; Zhu et al. 2026 (SCORE-style joint generation/evaluation, arXiv 2606.04507) [20]; Zhang et al. 2026 (Who grades the grader?, arXiv 2607.12790) [21]; Panickssery et al. (self-preference) [22]; Gou et al. 2024 (CRITIC) [60]. Appendix H names closest related work as SCORE [20], EvoRubrics [59], CURE [19], and Zhang et al. [21].

CODE
- p.31 Listing 1 (node 66): `- IMO_PROOF_REVISION_ENABLED = os.environ.get("HYPERAGENTS_IMO_PROOF_REVISION", "1") != "0"` replaced by `+ ... ("HYPERAGENTS_IMO_PROOF_REVISION", "0") == "1"`.
- p.19 Algorithm 1 key lines: gate `ExpandGate(T,N)`; checkpoint loop `Gamma_m <- {E[m]} U Challengers(m,T); BB[e] <- SlotBB_eps(e; GT[m],P[m]); e* <- Best(Gamma_m, BB; tie=E[m]); if e* != E[m]: P[m] <- AcceptedGenerations(E[m]); j[m]++; E[m] <- Freeze(e*); EraseSlotRecords(T,m); RecomputeCMPStats(T)`.
- p.37 BB_eps(e) = I^{-1}_eps(1+S_gt_e, 1+F_gt_e), the eps-quantile of Beta.

FIGURES (not captioned via script; from text)
- Fig 8 (p.20): expanded view of the RQGM loop (frozen evaluator per epoch, geometric checkpoints, erase on replacement). Best single picture of the mechanism.
- Fig 9 (p.21): anchor evidence persists, slot-local records erased; per-domain anchors.
- Fig 10 (p.28): token cost split. Fig 12 (p.29): 13x cheaper Nemotron. Fig 13 (p.32): leaderboard survival vs churn at each replacement. Fig 14 (p.33): DeepSWE archives.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Equation extraction is garbled in places (Greek letters, subscripts) but statements are readable. Tab. 15's last row prints 35.0% / 20.8% for the final reviewer, which differs from the prose (47% passing, 19% failing); that is probably a different patch subset (298 vs 337), and I did not reconcile it. The last row's "Patches" and "Failing" columns are fused ("1181 298"), so the exact counts are ambiguous. I did not read pp. 1-9 or verify main-text claims.
